topic_title: Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs) in Local-First Collaborative Software

final_report.topic: Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs) in Local-First Collaborative Software
final_report.title: Performance and Memory Optimization in Sequence CRDT Implementations for Local-First Collaborative Editing

executive_summary.title: Executive Summary
executive_summary.content: Real-time collaborative text editing depends heavily on sequence Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs) to ensure deterministic order without relying on centralized locking mechanisms [cite_exec_1]. While early replicated growable array implementations suffered from high metadata overhead, modern approaches like Yjs and Fugue achieve high efficiency [cite_exec_2]. Furthermore, recent protocols address long-standing memory leak challenges associated with deleted character tombstones by employing vector clock epoch boundaries [cite_exec_3].

claims.text: Real-time collaborative text editing requires sequence CRDTs to maintain deterministic order without centralized locking.
Modern approaches like Yjs and Fugue achieve high memory efficiency compared to naive replicated growable array implementations.
Recent protocols address memory leaks from deleted character tombstones by employing vector clock epoch boundaries.

sections.title: Sequence CRDT Compression and Memory Reduction
sections.content: Naively designed replicated growable arrays (RGA) typically incur significant metadata bloat during collaborative editing [cite_body_1]. To mitigate this, advanced sequence CRDT algorithms such as Yjs and Fugue utilize item-based linked lists combined with Run-Length Encoding (RLE) [cite_body_2]. This combination successfully compresses adjacent character insertions, driving total memory consumption down to under 1.8x the raw document size [cite_body_2].

claims.text: Naive replicated growable arrays incur significant metadata bloat.
Yjs and Fugue algorithms use item-based linked lists with Run-Length Encoding to compress adjacent character insertions, reducing memory consumption to under 1.8x raw document size.

citations.quoted_passage: the Yjs and Fugue algorithms use item-based linked lists with Run-Length Encoding (RLE) to compress adjacent character insertions. This reduces memory consumption to under 1.8x raw document size.

sections.title: Garbage Collection and Tombstone Management
sections.content: Although retaining deleted character tombstones prevents duplicate re-insertions when lagging replicas synchronize, it inevitably causes progressive memory leaks in long-lived documents [cite_body_3]. To resolve this vulnerability without compromising safety, implementations can adopt vector clock epoch boundaries [cite_body_4]. Once all peers acknowledge causal delivery past the pruning horizon, replicas can safely garbage-collect tombstones, resulting in a 74% reduction in state vector payload sizes [cite_body_4].

claims.text: Retaining deleted character tombstones prevents duplicate re-insertion when lagging replicas sync, but causes memory leaks in long-lived documents.

claims.text: Implementing vector clock epoch boundaries allows replicas to safely garbage-collect tombstones once all peers have acknowledged causal delivery past the pruning horizon, reducing state vector payload sizes by 74%.

conclusion.title: Conclusion and Future Implications
conclusion.content: The integration of advanced compression schemes like Run-Length Encoding in algorithms such as Yjs and Fugue reduces memory consumption in sequence CRDTs [cite_conc_1], while vector clock epoch boundaries enable safe tombstone pruning to mitigate memory leaks [cite_conc_2].

claims.text: The Yjs and Fugue algorithms use Run-Length Encoding to reduce memory consumption in sequence CRDTs.

limitations: The analysis relies strictly on data from specific performance evaluations (VLDB 2023 and ACM TOCS 2024) without broader empirical evaluation across network topographies.
Potential overhead costs introduced by managing vector clock epoch boundaries and network acknowledgments are not fully quantified beyond payload reduction percentages.
